name: Kretschmer constitutional types

lead: German psychiatrist Ernst Kretschmer sorted people into body-build types: asthenic (slight), athletic (muscular), pyknic (stocky, fuller) and dysplastic (mixed or disproportionate). He tied these to temperaments, such as cyclothymic and schizothymic.

For appearance-minded readers it is a historical root of the later ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph vocabulary. It gives a language for describing frame and build, which people use when thinking about how clothes, training and body fat sit on their physique.

paras: It is used as a descriptive vocabulary: people identify which build type they resemble and discuss it when planning training, clothing fit or bulking and cutting. It is not a test or a procedure.

The typology was developed in clinical psychiatry and its claims about build and personality were later criticised and are not treated as predictive. Its era was entangled with eugenics-related thinking, and modern personality psychology no longer relies on it.

chain: Match training, fat loss and clothing choices to the build
angle.text: The typology gives people words for their frame so they can discuss which parts of a physique are structural and which are changeable by training. In looksmaxxing talk it is mostly a historical reference to later somatotype ideas.

lead: Kretschmer's constitutional typology is a classification of human physique introduced by the German psychiatrist Ernst Kretschmer (1888-1964) in his 1921 book Körperbau und Charakter, published in English in 1931 as Physique and Character.[1] He described four main builds: asthenic, athletic, pyknic and dysplastic.[1]

The scheme matters to looks-oriented readers because it is an early attempt to name body shapes, and it sits upstream of the more familiar ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph categories proposed by William Sheldon in the 1940s.[2] Naming a build helps people think about proportion, frame and what training or fat loss will change.

Kretschmer himself was interested in psychiatry. He associated the pyknic build with cyclothymic temperament and the asthenic, athletic and dysplastic builds with schizothymic temperament, and related these to manic-depressive illness and schizophrenia.[1] Later historical reviews in psychiatry treat his work as part of the history of temperament research.[3][4]

paras: Asthenic builds are thin and small-framed, athletic builds are muscular and large-boned, pyknic builds are stocky and heavier, and dysplastic builds are disproportionate or mixed.[1]
Kretschmer saw cyclothymes (swinging between cheerful and sad) as often pyknic, while schizothymes (between sensitive and cold) were often athletic, asthenic or dysplastic.[1]

Kretschmer became director of the psychiatric clinic at Marburg University in 1926.[1] His typology was followed by William Sheldon's 1940s somatotypes (The Varieties of Human Physique, 1940; The Varieties of Temperament, 1942; Atlas of Men, 1954), which rated ectomorphy, mesomorphy and endomorphy on a 1-to-7 scale.[2] The Heath-Carter variant of Sheldon's method is still used in sports science and anthropometry.[2]

Historical papers in psychiatry cite Kretschmer in connection with schizophrenia, delusional disorder, dysthymia and affective temperaments.[3][4][5] A biographical piece describes how his ideas influenced the interwar psychiatrist Rafał Becker, who also held eugenic views.[6]

Wikipedia notes that the idea of linking body types to personality traits is no longer influential in personality psychology.[1] Sheldon's related work has been criticised for its methods and its eugenics-era context.[2]
No studies found. Kretschmer's temperament categories fed into later research on affective temperaments, which is reviewed in the psychiatric literature.[5]
